analysis.one_liner: Made gasoline and heating oil price gouging a federal offense with treble-damages penalties.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 389–34, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal unfair-practice violation to sell crude oil, gasoline, diesel, home heating oil, or biofuel at a gouging price, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules that define gouging. The FTC, the U.S. Attorney General, and state attorneys general could enforce it, with penalties of three times the overcharge plus daily fines, and criminal penalties for the worst cases. The House passed it the day after introduction by 389–34, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, truckers, and homes heated with fuel oil, who would gain a federal remedy when sellers charge far above fair market prices during shortages or crises. Civil penalty money — three times the overcharge — would flow into state funds that compensate consumers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes selling crude oil, gasoline, diesel, home heating oil, or biofuel at a price that constitutes gouging an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, giving consumers a federal backstop against opportunistic fuel prices.
Lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of their residents to stop the conduct, force compliance, and collect civil penalties.

Imposes penalties of three times the amount charged above the fair market price — up to $3 million per day for wholesale violations — and requires the overcharge portion to be deposited into state funds used to compensate consumers.
Adds criminal penalties for gouging: fines up to $150 million for wholesale violations and up to $2 million for retail, plus up to two years in prison.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, refiners, and fuel retailers, who would face treble-damages civil penalties, daily fines, and possible criminal prosecution for sales deemed gouging. Some of that cost could be passed through in prices at the margin.

drawbacks.text: The bill's central term — 'price gouging' — is not defined in the bill itself; the FTC must write the definition within six months, and drawing a line between unlawful gouging and legitimate price spikes driven by supply disruptions in a volatile commodity market is genuinely difficult.

Enforcement is exclusive to the FTC, the U.S. Attorney General, and state attorneys general, and state action is barred while a federal case is pending against the same defendant — no private lawsuits, and state enforcement pauses behind the federal government.
Heavy penalties on sellers during shortages could discourage fuel suppliers from moving product into an affected market, or be passed to customers in prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and the penalty structure — treble overcharge flowing into consumer compensation funds — is well targeted at the harm. The honest cost is that 'gouging' is hard to define, so the bill's usefulness depends heavily on how the FTC writes its rules, and the preemption of state action while a federal case is pending narrows who can act. On balance a consumer-protection bill with design questions rather than fatal flaws.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly under a fast-track procedure, the Senate put it on its calendar, and no senator ever got a vote on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Heather Wilson introduced the bill on May 2, 2006, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The very next day, May 3, 2006, Rep. Joe Barton moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill — a fast-track path requiring a two-thirds majority — and it passed 389–34.
The vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 190 of 230 Republicans and 198 of 201 Democrats voted yes; 33 Republicans and 1 Democrat voted no.
The Senate received the bill on May 4, 2006, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 5, 2006 — Calendar No. 461.
No Senate vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fuel sellers — refiners and retailers of gasoline, diesel, and heating oil — are better off, since the treble-damages penalties and criminal fines were never enacted. Drivers and heating-oil customers are left with no new federal protection against price gouging.

for.name: Rep. Heather Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 34 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill on the House floor the day after it was introduced.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to the Senate floor; it sat on the Senate calendar through the end of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 389–34 with near-unanimous support from both parties — 190 of 230 Republicans and 198 of 201 Democrats in favor, 33 Republicans and 1 Democrat opposed — and all 34 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill's failure was not a party-line vote but a Senate that never voted at all.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed wholesale sellers of crude oil, gasoline, diesel, and heating oil to penalties of three times the overcharge plus up to $3 million per day, and criminal fines up to $150 million. Their interest in blocking it ran against consumers paying the post-hurricane 2006 fuel prices. Because the bill died, these penalties never took effect.

Retail sellers faced three times the overcharge as a civil penalty and fines up to $2 million with two years' imprisonment for gouging at the pump. The bill's death leaves retail fuel pricing to state laws only.

Biofuels are swept into the same gouging prohibition, so sellers of ethanol and biodiesel would face the same penalties as oil sellers — but inclusion also prevents the ban from giving biofuels a price-gouging carve-out competitors could exploit.
